metadata.title: Delta Beats, Raises, and Sends You the Fuel Bill

content.text:
BREAKING NEWS
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
Delta opened airline earnings season Friday with a quarter that had every reason to be ugly and wasn't. Adjusted earnings of $1.56 per share beat the $1.48 expected, revenue of $17.67 billion topped estimates, and operating revenue jumped 19% from a year ago, all with war-inflated jet fuel gnawing at the cost line the entire quarter.
The guidance carries the confidence. Delta forecast third-quarter earnings of $2.00 to $2.50 per share against estimates of $2.02, sees revenue up mid-teens, and reaffirmed its full-year target of $6.50 to $7.50.
How is this possible with oil doing what oil did? Because you're paying. Airfares are up nearly 27% from last year, and CEO Ed Bastian says Delta has passed along about 60% of its higher fuel bill so far, headed for "close to 100%" this quarter. Demand is absorbing it, helped by a stronger-than-expected World Cup and rebounding corporate travel.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
And this quarter delivered a genuine milestone in Delta's longest-running project: the premium cabins out-earned coach, $6.92 billion to $6.85 billion. Delta has spent a decade methodically turning itself into a luxury product with an economy section attached, adding seat tiers and courting the traveler who pays for legroom without checking the price. That bet is now literally the bigger business, and it's why Delta can raise fares into a K-shaped economy: its core customer is the K's upper stroke.
Not everything gleamed. Net income fell 25%, and unit costs rose faster than unit revenue. The oddball bright spot: Delta's Pennsylvania refinery, where revenue surged 83%, because owning a refinery during an oil war is a lovely hedge.
Bastian insists the pricing power outlasts the war, betting a disciplined industry won't flood back with cheap seats when oil falls. Airlines have promised that before. For now, the fares are sticking.
